newsitem.title: USA: H&R Block says open to CompuServe options.
newsitem.headline: H&R Block says open to CompuServe options.

text.p: H&R Block Inc said Wednesday that its cancellation of a vote on spinning off its interest in online service CompuServe Corp will allow it to explore other ways of disposing of the stake.

Earlier, H&R Block said its decision not to hold the vote at its September 11 annual meeting was based in part on CompuServe's reported first quarter and projected second quarter losses, as well as a September introduction of new interfaces for the online service.

"(I) think the board is saying it's withdrawing and wants the time to consider these other matters," said Linda McDougall, a spokeswoman for H&R Block. "It also leaves it open to other alternatives," she said.

McDougall said the board of directors does not have a deadline for deciding on a spinoff. The tax return preparation and financial services company said in a statement that it still believes a separation of CompuServe is in the best interests of H&R Block shareholders.
"I wouldn't want to speculate what the board might consider," McDougall said in an interview.
Shares of H&R Block fell 1-7/8 to 26 on the news, while CompuServe jumped 15/16 to 13-1/4.
"The stock took it hard because the stock market likes visibility and certainty and we lost a bit of that," said Alexander Paris, senior analysts with Barrington Research.
Paris said the vote cancellation also sets back company plans to repurchase up to 15 million H&R Block shares.
"The company cannot start to buy back shares until this is done," Paris said, citing regulatory issues.
Analysts said CompuServe was boosted by the news because the 74.2 million shares a spin-off would put in the market would have weighed hard on CompuServe's share price.
"The fact the spinoff was coming put added pressure on CompuServe," said Paul Mackey, an analyst for Dean Witter. "Many (H&R Block shareholders) were just going to sell it."

Kansas City-based H&R Block had proposed spinning off its 80 percent share in CompuServe, giving shareholders about seven CompuServe shares per 10 Block shares. The company recently said it expected the spin off to be completed on or around November 1, subject to the shareholder vote and authorization for a tax-free deal.
"I think right now the answer is obvious," Mackey said. "There is probably a reasonable alternative that would be better than the spinoff."
The analysts said H&R Block may be better off looking for a company to acquire CompuServe.
"I think it's definitely a possibility," Paris said.
